I. INTRODUCTION
arXiv:2509.13737v1  [cs.RO]  17 Sep 2025
Achieving adaptive maneuver for legged robots closing
to their real life counterparts in unstructured environments
has been a long-term goal in the legged robot community.
Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a cutting-edge
control method for legged robot locomotion in recent years,
and existing work has validated its flexibility in various
real-world environments [1], [2], [3], [4]. However, the
RL control paradigm suffers from significant performance
degradation in out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions, as RL
policies only have limited generalization ability in the regions
near the state distributions that they have explored during
training, and control performance becomes unreliable in
unforeseen environments that differ from the pre-explored
space.
Legged locomotion typically involves two levels of control
requirements. On the one hand, the controller must account
for diverse contact forces to maintain balance during the
stance phase. On the other hand, it must perform gait
planning and adapt leg motions to abrupt state change (e.g.,
base velocity) and diverse terrains during the swing phase.
However, in RL pipelines, these two objectives are tightly
coupled: The action commands sent to the PD controller
are expected to simultaneously generate appropriate reaction
forces and leg movements. While this coupling simplifies
controller specification, it substantially enlarges the state ex-
ploration space by forcing the policy to balance two distinct
objectives, thereby increasing both the difficulty and cost of
learning. More critically, in our view, this coupling is a key
reason for the discrepancy between simulation and reality

[Literature Review] Dynamic Adaptive Legged Locomotion Policy via Decoupling Reaction Force Control and Gait Control

AI Achieve unprecedented robustness and tackle sim-to-real challenges in legged robots with this novel, decoupled MPC-RL framework.

Image: review-image

This paper introduces a novel decoupled control framework designed to enhance the robustness and adaptability of legged robot locomotion policies, particularly in out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions and for mitigating the sim-to-real gap. Unlike traditional Reinforcement Learning (RL) approaches where reaction force control and gait control are tightly coupled, the proposed method separates these objectives, assigning stance-leg control (reaction forces) to an online Model Predictive Control (MPC) module and swing-leg control (gait motion tracking) to an RL policy.

The core motivation stems from the observation that tightly coupled control objectives in RL lead to enlarged state exploration spaces, increased learning difficulty, and a more pronounced sim-to-real gap due to the delicate balance required between force and position control. Domain randomization (DR) is a common but often sub-optimal solution, as it sacrifices optimality for individual environments to achieve broader generalization. The decoupled approach aims to provide fast online adaptation by allowing the reaction force to be adjusted by MPC without interfering with leg motion commands from RL.

The system overview details two main modules: MPC and RL. During training, the MPC module generates offline dynamics and kinematics trajectories (joint torques, positions, velocities, contact sequences). The joint torque trajectories are used as feedforward input to a low-level controller (LLC), while motion references guide the RL agent's learning. During deployment, the MPC runs online at a high frequency (500 Hz) to provide real-time feedforward joint torques and motion references, while the RL policy runs at a lower frequency (50 Hz) to track the gait.

The Robust MPC component utilizes a Chance-Constraint MPC (CCMPC) from prior work, which optimizes ground reaction forces (GRF) and provides reference motion. CCMPC explicitly incorporates uncertainties (e.g., payloads, terrains) by modeling them as probability distributions, allowing for a small, acceptable probability of constraint violation. It employs a stochastic variation of the Single Rigid Body Dynamics (SRBD) model, expressed as a discrete linear state-space equation:

$$x_{i+1} = A_i x_i + B_i(\delta_i) u_i + w_i$$x i+1​=A i​x i​+B i​(δ i​)u i​+w i​Image

The optimization problem is formulated as a Quadratic Program (QP) and includes chance constraints for friction cones and unilateral forces:

An additional constraint $D_i u_i = 0$D i​u i​=0 ensures zero GRFs for swing legs. Experiments were conducted on a Unitree Go2 quadruped robot in simulation (Isaac Gym, Pybullet) and hardware. Baselines included an RL policy trained with a nominal PD controller and another with additional Domain Randomization (DR). The proposed method demonstrated:

  1. Effectiveness of Decoupled Framework: In simulation, the method showed a smaller gap between joint actions and joint positions in the stance phase compared to baselines, indicating that the RL policy primarily outputs decoupled kinematics. The feedforward torque from MPC dynamically adapted to a 10 kg payload, confirming online adaptation. It achieved faster learning convergence and superior sim-to-real transfer, with significantly lower velocity tracking RMSE in Pybullet and the real world (0.13 $\pm$± 0.08 m/s compared to 0.20 $\pm$± 0.07 m/s for Baseline-DR).
  2. Robustness to Horizontal Disturbances: The method resisted substantially higher horizontal forces (e.g., 105 N from front, 75 N from back, 40 N from side) with lower velocity RMSE compared to baselines (e.g., 60 N max for baseline from front).
  3. Locomotion on Complex Terrains: It traversed more challenging terrains, handling higher uneven terrain ranges (0.07 m vs. 0.06 m for Baseline-DR) and steeper slopes (13 degrees vs. 7 degrees for Baseline-DR), maintaining better velocity tracking.
  4. Hardware Experiments with Payloads:
     * Heavy Payloads: Achieved 100% success rate with payloads up to 7.5 kg (vs. 0% for baselines), demonstrating a linear increase in mean calf feedforward torque with payload weight, and maintaining gait consistency.
     * Biased Payloads: Successfully carried 7.5 kg biased payloads (shifted 7 cm along the y-axis), where baselines failed at 2.5 kg, showing superior tracking of commanded velocity (e.g., RMSE for $v_x$v x​ 0.05 $\pm$± 0.03 m/s for 7.5 kg biased payload) and more stable base orientation.

In conclusion, the decoupled framework, by isolating reaction force control via online MPC and gait motion tracking via RL, achieves efficient learning, significantly reduces the sim-to-real gap, and provides robust dynamic adaptation to various unforeseen disturbances and environments with minimal domain randomization. Future work includes exploring more flexible swing trajectory generators.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Title: CDFlow: Generative Gradient Flows for Configuration Space Distance Fields via Neural ODEs
Authors: Mengzhu Li, Yunyu Zhou, He Ying, F. Richard Yu
Date: Wed Sep 17 07:38:47 2025

Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) are a fundamental representation in robot motion planning. Their configuration-space counterpart, the Configuration Space Distance Field (CDF), directly encodes distances in joint space, offering a unified representation for optimization and control. However, existing CDF formulations face two major challenges in high-degree-of-freedom (DoF) robots: (1) they effectively return only a single nearest collision configuration, neglecting the multi-modal nature of minimal-distance collision configurations and leading to gradient ambiguity; and (2) they rely on sparse sampling of the collision boundary, which often fails to identify the true closest configurations, producing oversmoothed approximations and geometric distortion in high-dimensional spaces. We propose CDFlow, a novel framework that addresses these limitations by learning a continuous flow in configuration space via Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (Neural ODEs). We redefine the problem from finding a single nearest point to modeling the distribution of minimal-distance collision configurations. We also introduce an adaptive refinement sampling strategy to generate high-fidelity training data for this distribution. The resulting Neural ODE implicitly models this multi-modal distribution and produces a smooth, consistent gradient field-derived as the expected direction towards the distribution-that mitigates gradient ambiguity and preserves sharp geometric features. Extensive experiments on high-DoF motion planning tasks demonstrate that CDFlow significantly improves planning efficiency, trajectory quality, and robustness compared to existing CDF-based methods, enabling more robust and efficient planning for collision-aware robots in complex environments.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

> Abstract:Trustworthy trajectory prediction grounds autonomous vehicle (AV) safety, yet deployed models inevitably face out-of-distribution (OOD) scenes. Prior AV OOD detection targets perception, but planners act on predicted futures rather than raw scenes, so erroneous forecasts can slip past frame-level checks and corrupt control. We therefore tackle OOD detection at the trajectory-prediction level. Our analysis of real-world benchmarks reveals that prediction errors are often multi-modal, exhibiting distinct low- and high-error modes that evolve with open-world driving context. Observing this, we propose Mode-Aware CUSUM, which explicitly models multiple error modes while retaining the efficiency and general compatibility of classical CUSUM. By dynamically identifying the active error mode and adapting detection thresholds, our method enables robust monitoring across heterogeneous conditions. Experiments on large-scale trajectory benchmarks demonstrate consistent reductions in detection delay and false alarms.

Title: Dynamic Aware: Adaptive Multi-Mode Out-of-Distribution Detection for Trajectory Prediction in Autonomous Vehicles
Authors: Tongfei Guo, Lili Su
Date: Tue Sep 16 22:37:21 2025

Trajectory prediction is central to the safe and seamless operation of autonomous vehicles (AVs). In deployment, however, prediction models inevitably face distribution shifts between training data and real-world conditions, where rare or underrepresented traffic scenarios induce out-of-distribution (OOD) cases. While most prior OOD detection research in AVs has concentrated on computer vision tasks such as object detection and segmentation, trajectory-level OOD detection remains largely underexplored. A recent study formulated this problem as a quickest change detection (QCD) task, providing formal guarantees on the trade-off between detection delay and false alarms [1]. Building on this foundation, we propose a new framework that introduces adaptive mechanisms to achieve robust detection in complex driving environments. Empirical analysis across multiple real-world datasets reveals that prediction errors -- even on in-distribution samples -- exhibit mode-dependent distributions that evolve over time with dataset-specific dynamics. By explicitly modeling these error modes, our method achieves substantial improvements in both detection delay and false alarm rates. Comprehensive experiments on established trajectory prediction benchmarks show that our framework significantly outperforms prior UQ- and vision-based OOD approaches in both accuracy and computational efficiency, offering a practical path toward reliable, driving-aware autonomy.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

> 摘要: Training reinforcement learning (RL) policies for legged locomotion often requires extensive environment interactions, which are costly and time-consuming. We propose Symmetry-Guided Memory Augmentation (SGMA), a framework that improves training efficiency by combining structured experience augmentation with memory-based context inference. Our method leverages robot and task symmetries to generate additional, physically consistent training experiences without requiring extra interactions. To avoid the pitfalls of naive augmentation, we extend these transformations to the policy's memory states, enabling the agent to retain task-relevant context and adapt its behavior accordingly. We evaluate the approach on quadruped and humanoid robots in simulation, as well as on a real quadruped platform. Across diverse locomotion tasks involving joint failures and payload variations, our method achieves efficient policy training while maintaining robust performance, demonstrating a practical route toward data-efficient RL for legged robots.
